summary: Extends the BGP Flow Specification mechanism of RFC 8955 to IPv6 traffic. It defines IPv6-specific encodings for describing traffic flows to filter or rate-limit, and updates the IANA Flow Spec Component Types registry accordingly.

eli5.summary: The same shared filter-rule system for routers, now taught to describe the newer kind of Internet addresses, too.

questions: how to filter ipv6 traffic using bgp flow specification
what is bgp flowspec for ipv6
what is the flow label component in flowspec
subtitle: How BGP Flow Specification learns to describe IPv6 traffic, with new components, a prefix offset and a new redirect action.

tldr.problem: BGP Flow Specification (RFC 8955) only described IPv4 packets, so operators had no standard way to spread filtering and rate-limiting rules for IPv6 traffic.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8956 defines the changes needed for IPv6: the (AFI=2, SAFI=133 or 134) address family pair, IPv6 prefix components with an offset, a new Flow Label component, a changed validation rule and a new IPv6 redirect action.
tldr.outcome: IPv6 flows can be matched and acted on the same way as IPv4 ones. It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 8955 by merging IPv4 and IPv6 component types into one IANA registry.

today: RFC 8956 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 8955 and extends it to IPv6.

sections.title: Why IPv6 Needs Its Own Flow Specification
sections.content:
RFC 8955 provides a BGP extension for spreading traffic flow information so that routers can rate limit or filter IPv4 packets. This document, RFC 8956, extends it to IPv6. The text notes that the growing amount of IPv6 traffic requires tools used in IPv4-only networks to support IPv6 data packets too.

RFC 8956 is deliberately a delta. It only defines the changes needed for IPv6, and everything else about Flow Specification stays in RFC 8955 and is not repeated. It also updates RFC 8955 by changing the IANA Flow Spec Component Types registry.
sections.eli5: It is like adding a new chapter to an existing rulebook instead of writing a whole new book. Only the new parts are written down.

sections.title: Carrying IPv6 Rules in BGP
sections.content:
RFC 8955 defines SAFI 133 (Dissemination of Flow Specification rules) and SAFI 134 (L3VPN Dissemination of Flow Specification rules). To exchange IPv6 Flow Specifications, implementations MUST advertise the Multiprotocol Extension Capability (Code 1) from RFC 4760.

The (AFI, SAFI) pair in that capability MUST be (AFI=2, SAFI=133) for IPv6 Flow Specification rules and (AFI=2, SAFI=134) for the L3VPN variant.
sections.eli5: Two routers first agree out loud that they will swap IPv6 filter rules. Only then do they start sending them.

sections.title: IPv6 Flow Specification Components
sections.content:
Each component starts with a 1-octet Type followed by a variable-length parameter. Types 4 (Port), 5 (Destination Port), 6 (Source Port), 9 (TCP Flags), 10 (Packet Length) and 11 (DSCP) from RFC 8955 apply to IPv6 unchanged.

The prefix components, Type 1 (Destination IPv6 Prefix) and Type 2 (Source IPv6 Prefix), are encoded as type, length, offset, pattern and padding. The offset says how many most significant address bits to skip before matching starts, and length is the bit position where matching stops. This helps when part of an IPv6 address holds an embedded IPv4 address. A length of 0 with offset 0 matches every address; otherwise length MUST satisfy offset < length < 129 or the component is malformed. Padding bits MUST be 0 on encoding and ignored on decoding.

Other components are redefined for IPv6:

  • Type 3, Upper-Layer Protocol: matches the first Next Header value that is not an extension header. Values SHOULD be a single octet.
  • Type 7 and Type 8, ICMPv6 Type and Code: match only ICMPv6 packets, meaning upper-layer protocol 58. They never match a non-first fragment or a packet whose transport header cannot be located.
  • Type 12, Fragment: a single-octet bitmask with flags IsF (a fragment other than the first), FF (first fragment) and LF (last fragment), based on the IPv6 Fragment Header.
  • Type 13, Flow Label (new): matches the 20-bit Flow Label header field. Values SHOULD be 4-octet quantities.
sections.eli5: A rule is built from small pieces such as 'comes from this street' or 'is this kind of message'. IPv6 gets a few new pieces, including one for a special label stuck on each packet.

sections.title: Worked Encoding Examples
sections.content:
The RFC walks through two byte-level examples. In the first, a rule matches packets from ::1234:5678:9a00:0/64-104 to 2001:db8::/32 with upper-layer protocol TCP. The NLRI length is 18 octets (0x12). The source component has length 104 bits and offset 64 bits, so its pattern is 40 bits, which ends on an octet boundary and needs no padding.

In the second, the source is /65-104. The pattern is 104 - 65 = 39 bits, so one bit of padding is added to end on an octet boundary, and the NLRI length is 15 octets (0x0f).
sections.eli5: The examples show exactly which bytes go on the wire for a rule. If the pattern does not fill the last byte, the leftover bit is filled with a zero.

sections.title: Ordering and Validation
sections.content:
Rule ordering reuses Section 5.1 of RFC 8955 with a new consideration for the prefix offset. When offsets are equal, the comparison is the same and keeps longest-prefix-match semantics. When offsets differ, the lowest offset has precedence, because that rule matches the most significant bit. Appendix A gives a Python 3 implementation of the comparison.

Validation follows Section 6 of RFC 8955, except that item a) now reads: a destination prefix component with offset=0 is embedded in the Flow Specification.
sections.eli5: When two rules could both apply, there is a tie-break: the one that starts looking at the front of the address wins.

sections.title: The IPv6 Redirect Action
sections.content:
The traffic filtering actions from RFC 8955 can be applied to IPv6 flows. To support an IPv6-address-specific route target, a new action called rt-redirect-ipv6, Type 0x000d, is defined.

It redirects traffic to a VRF routing instance that lists the specified IPv6-Address-Specific Route-Target in its import policy. If several local instances match, the choice between them is a local matter. The encoding follows the IPv6-Address-Specific Route-Target Extended Community of RFC 5701 with the Type always 0x000d. It interferes with all BGP Flow Specification redirect actions, including itself.
sections.eli5: Besides 'block' or 'slow down', a rule can say 'send this traffic down a different road'. This adds a version of that instruction for the longer addresses.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 8955 now also apply to IPv6 networks. The RFC adds that oversized IPv6 header chains (RFC 7112) and wrongly formatted packets can keep a Type 3 component from being enforced. Hardware limitations in several routers may also make it impossible to enforce rules that match on upper-layer properties.

IANA now keeps IPv4 and IPv6 Flow Specification component types in a single Flow Spec Component Types registry, and assigned 0x000d for rt-redirect-ipv6 in the Transitive IPv6-Address-Specific Extended Community Types registry. Type 13 (Flow Label) is IPv6 only.
sections.eli5: Some odd or broken packets, and some older router hardware, can slip past certain rules. IANA keeps one list of all rule piece numbers.
